stem:
An ICU registrar reviews a 61-year-old who remains unconscious 18 hours after return of spontaneous circulation following a cardiac arrest. Oxygenation and blood pressure are within targets. The chest radiograph shows a small right basal opacity, and a sputum sample has been sent. Core temperature has risen to 38.6°C.

Which temperature plan is most appropriate?

options.label: A
options.text: Observe the temperature, as early post-arrest fever is expected
options.explanation: Fever is common after cardiac arrest but is associated with worse neurological outcome. It should be prevented, not simply observed.

options.label: B
options.text: Give paracetamol only if the temperature exceeds 39.5°C
options.explanation: Waiting for 39.5°C allows exactly the fever that post-arrest care aims to prevent.

options.label: C
options.text: Treat the fever with antibiotics as the temperature plan
options.explanation: Antibiotics may be appropriate if pneumonia is suspected, but they do not control temperature. The fever itself needs active management.

options.label: D
options.text: Allow the fever so that neurological examination is reliable
options.explanation: Fever does not make the neurological examination more reliable. Prognostication is delayed and multimodal regardless.

options.label: E
options.text: Start active temperature control to prevent further fever
options.explanation: In patients who remain unconscious after cardiac arrest, fever should be actively prevented, for at least 72 hours, using antipyretics and cooling devices as needed.

context: Actively prevent fever in patients who remain comatose after cardiac arrest, whatever its cause.
